As he climbed with the friends who had brought him, he began to spot monarchs along the path. Only a few at first. But the higher he went, the more he heard a sound in the background, like something whispering in the trees. Suddenly, a swarm of butterflies was flying overhead, millions of orange and black wings fluttering against the blue sky beyond. “There were so many that you could feel a slight breeze when they flew over you,” he says. Here are the best places to eat the prized bivalves. The Pacific ‘rock’ oyster and the European native ‘flat’ oyster are the two main types of oysters consumed in the UK. Falmouth Oyster Festival By Davey Brett Published September 2, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). If you ever need an excuse to eat an oyster, Bobby Groves has plenty. The author of Oyster Isles: A Journey Through Britain and Ireland’s Oysters — a book written on a 5,000-mile motorcycle ride across the UK and Ireland charting the oyster industry and its heritage — has more than 20 years’ experience in the industry and makes a compelling argument for their consumption. “I think people want something hyper-local, something [with flavour] that reflects the environment, something that can help fight climate change and is very healthy to eat,” Bobby says. The humble oyster ticks all four boxes, each one filtering surrounding waters, developing its own unique flavour and trapping nitrogen and carbon in its shell. Two main types of oyster are consumed in the UK. The Pacific ‘rock’ oyster and the European native ‘flat’ oyster. Both are bivalve molluscs, but the two differ in origin, taste and shape. pages.text: Itemized deductions, standard deduction | Internal Revenue Service Skip to main content Itemized deductions, standard deduction More In Help Interactive Tax Assistant Tools Report fraud Tax scams Identity theft Notices and letters Appeals Frequently asked questions Accessibility Contact your local IRS office Contact an international IRS office Tax topics Other languages Top Frequently Asked Questions for Itemized Deductions, Standard Deduction If I must deduct points over the life of my mortgage, and I have a 30-year mortgage, should I divide the points paid by 30 and enter that amount on Schedule A of Form 1040? Answer: No. While you must deduct the points over the life of the loan ratably (equally), you don't divide the points by 30 years. Instead, you divide the points by the number of payments scheduled over the term of the loan (360 monthly payments in the case of a 30-year mortgage) and deduct points each year according to the number of payments you made in that year (less than twelve payments in some cases). If the loan ends prematurely, for example, because you paid it off or refinanced with a different lender, then the remaining points are deductible in that year. Note: This does not apply to loans refinanced with the same lender. Any deductible points not included on Form 1098 (usually not included on the Form when refinancing) should be entered on Schedule A (Form 1040), Itemized Deductions , line 8c "Points not reported to you on Form 1098." Close j333-1145's Diary osm 极简画法 Posted by j333-1145 on 3 May 2026 in Chinese (China) (‪中文(中国大陆)‬) . 前言 这些随想是在去年年底写的，也许对其他 mapper 有启发，故发布。 以下经验会让画 osm 变得高效、美观、简洁，避免 无线细化 。 正文 osm 本质是抽象、简化的地图，所以画面元素要少、整洁。增加过多的元素会导致地图画面杂乱无章、不美观，而且后期维护也很繁琐。 例：一条公路的两旁有人行道，除非有物理隔离（比如栏杆），否则推荐在道路上加 sidewalk=both ，而不是把两旁的人行道都画出来 要提炼出对象特征，想出表达完整又简练的画面布局，同时不要出现渲染错误。 直线要直、圆形要园、方形要方、弧线要优雅大气。 线条不宜有过多节点，尽量把多余的、又不影响整体的节点删掉 道路、河流、森林等图画，宜大不宜小，宜长不宜短，宜整不宜碎 能不重叠就不重叠。如果一片区域（比如小区、医院、学校等），有明确的边界（比如围墙），最好先画完内部道路、建筑设施，最后再画上土地利用 area=yes 。否则就不要画。 一般使用 iD 编辑器最简单。若想画整齐的方形建筑物建议用 JOSM，并使用 building 插件。 标签方面，非必要不多加。 Discussion Comment from 真中あお on 3 July 2026 at 09:23 提醒自己地图是对现实的抽象，不追求无限细化，这是很有意义的方法论d(`･∀･)b Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

He was 83. The cause was congestive heart failure, Lydia DeJohnette, his wife and manager, tells NPR. DeJohnette had a singular voice at the drums: earthy and elastic, instantly recognizable. He adapted this flowing approach from modern jazz innovators like Roy Haynes as well as avant-garde pioneers like Rashied Ali , devising what he called a multidirectional style. But when play resumed, he was everywhere. Tackling, scrambling, hitting the deck and springing back up. By the final whistle, Botham had helped Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years. He was man of the match. And as the celebrations began, the tears flowed. Quite an afternoon for a player accustomed to working away from the spotlight. DeWitt characterized people of Japanese ancestry during World War II. Close jfd553's Diary Mapping Icefields Parkway, Part 1: A two-year mapping journey Posted by jfd553 on 4 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 6 November 2026. I spent two years mapping the areas surrounding one of the most beautiful drives in the world. Each morning, I looked forward to discovering and mapping an area adjacent to a one I did the day before. This diary entry serves as an introduction to a series of texts covering the challenges I encountered and how I overcame them. Included below are a few snapshots taken in the field, which capture the majestic landscapes along the Icefields Parkway. I have also added a “before and after” map excerpt, as well as a short video, to illustrate how my work gradually took shape over time. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. The parkway, which is a 232 km stretch of highway cutting through Banff and Jasper National Parks, attracts between 1.2 million and 2 million visitors per year. The parkway offers exceptional alpine landscape, with glaciers, rivers, turquoise lakes, and breathtaking mountain views directly from the roadside (Figure 1). Best of all, many of these landmarks can be reached in a single day’s hike (Figure 2). Figure 1: North Saskatchewan River alongside the parkway. Veils of seaweed hung from its rotting timbers, and it was encrusted with barnacles. The insides were full of mud. Richard Mukuze By Sam Kemp Published November 18, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The jazz saxophonist Stan Getz once said that the best music sounds “like a good conversation among friends”. Right now, some of the most interesting musical conversations in London are happening at its grassroots venues, where open jam sessions are giving musicians of all levels a platform to improvise, hone their craft and form new friendships. Participants may not know their fellow musicians, let alone the genre or dynamic, so there’s no choice but to embrace whatever the night brings. It’s about getting lost in music, together. London’s open jam scene really took hold in the years following the Covid lockdown — a period when music-lovers were looking for new ways to connect in a city beset by independent venue closures and the ongoing effects of social isolation. pages.text: Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand | National Geographic TRAVEL Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand A new off-grid tour takes travellers deep into New Zealand’s largest basin in search of the elusive black stilt. New Zealand's Southern Alps are home to one of the world's rarest birds: the black stilt. Natasha Bazika By Natasha Bazika Published June 11, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Clouds move quickly across the Mackenzie Basin, dragging shadows over braided riverbeds and dry tussock plains that stretch towards New Zealand’s Southern Alps. One moment, the landscape is washed silver; the next, it disappears beneath a sweep of weather rolling over the mountains. I’m heading deeper into this high country on a window of borrowed time, crossing the 46,950-acre wilderness of Glenmore Station, a merino sheep, deer and cattle station. Hours earlier, the same storm front had grounded my helicopter flight to the country’s highest whisky bar — The Bad Decision, on a saddle above Glenmore Station — before it could leave the tarmac. Now, I’m racing a temporary clearing in the weather to find something far more elusive than a dram of mountain liquor: the black stilt, or kakī in Māori, one of the rarest birds on the planet. “The Mackenzie Basin has its own weather system,” says guide Ben Laffan, who’s taking me on Tekapo Adventures’ Black Stilt birding tour , a newly launched birdwatching experience, directing our four-wheel drive up a rough track. pages.description: The animals that plummeted 85 feet into Wyoming’s Natural Trap Cave provide a layered history of life dating back to the Pleistocene
pages.text: Journey Into a Prehistoric Cave That Trapped and Entombed Animals for Millennia Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Photos courtesy of Dr. Susumu Tomiya and public domain Natural Trap Cave is a pit in northern Wyoming into which countless animals have fallen and met their untimely demise since the Pleistocene. Paleontologists today find the cave a treasure trove — a stunning record of the species that have long roamed the area. The mammalian fossils left behind shed light on the climate, food sources and migration patterns of these species from earlier eras. Careful excavation work over the years that has involved sifting for bones, extracting ancient DNA, and looking for prehistoric pollen has revealed not just the plants and animals that once populated this part of the world, but also the ecosystems and climates that governed it. It also has required some rather advanced rappelling skills. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with vertebrate paleontologist Julie Meachen and Smithsonian contributing writer Michael Ray Taylor about what rappelling into Natural Trap Cave reveals about its contents and what it can tell us about Earth’s past. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/keepers-right-answer-why-measurements-nist-are-important-nation-and-world Taking Measure Just a Standard Blog Keepers of the Right Answer: Why Measurements at NIST Are Important for the Nation and the World September 11, 2024 By: James K. Olthoff Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email James K. Olthoff is NIST’s first chief metrologist. Credit: NIST Practically everything you use in your everyday life works because of measurement science. pages.description: Usman Khawaja's autobiography has exposed the limbo Australian cricket finds itself stuck in over the sandpaper scandal, writes Stephan Shemilt.
pages.text: Khawaja book: Sandpapergate a stench Cricket Australia cannot shake - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pat Cummins has led Australia in 43 Tests since 2021 By Stephan Shemilt Cricket Correspondent Published 10 November 2026 There are stories that can damage reputations, tarnish legacies and put asterisks next to achievements. Never-ending sagas, claim and counterclaim, one word against another. Are Pep Guardiola's trophies at Manchester City rendered worthless by financial rule breaches? Would either of the Houston Astros or Boston Red Sox have won the World Series without sign stealing? How much fake blood was spilled by Harlequins? Now, sandpapergate has morphed into Usman Khawaja's-book-gate, opening old wounds and asking questions that have hung over Australian cricket since Cameron Bancroft hid some DIY equipment in his jockstrap in 2018. Published on Tuesday, Khawaja's autobiography – Sabr – is only suggesting what plenty have suspected for the past eight years. It always seemed likely that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were not the only three members of the Australia camp with knowledge of the sandpaper plot. Careful with his words, perhaps for legal reasons, Khawaja has said enough to reignite a row that once consumed the entire nation of Australia. Crucially, the former batter has not named individuals and, in the opinion of Cricket Australia (CA), not presented enough evidence to merit a new investigation. Cybersecurity Career Week (CCW) , a campaign led by the NICE Program at NIST from October 19-24, 2026, aims to raise public awareness and help people find their path to #ChooseCyber. During this week, academia, industry, non-profit organizations, and government agencies host events, share resources, provide trainings, and engage community to build awareness about the cybersecurity job opportunities, educate people on how to develop capabilities to qualify for cybersecurity roles, and showcase how building a cybersecurity workforce enhances the Nation’s security and promotes economic prosperity. How to get started Be ready to engage, explore, and try something new. Use CCW to ask questions, attend an event, connect with people already working in the field, or participate in challenges.
